title: 📘 UNIT 8: POLITICAL, SOCIAL AND ECONOMIC PROCESSES IN ETHIOPIA, MID-16TH TO MID-19TH CENTURY
notes: ⏳ Period → mid-16th to mid-19th century.

title: 8.1 🏘️ Peoples and States of Southern, Western and Eastern Ethiopia
notes:
Southern, western and eastern Ethiopia contained many peoples with long traditions of political organization and state formation.

Major indigenous institutions → Tato system + Kawo/Kati system + Sera-Woma system + Gadaa-related institutions + councils of elders.

📌 Common foundations → agriculture + pastoralism + trade + handicrafts + indigenous law + traditional leadership.

📌 Trade and Islam became important forces in the rise and prosperity of several states.

title: 8.1.1 🌿 Southern States — Omotic Peoples
notes:
Omotic peoples → mainly lived around both sides of the Omo River.

Language → Omotic belongs to the Afro-Asiatic super-family and is spoken only in Ethiopia.

Major economic activities → enset cultivation + agriculture + pastoralism + handicrafts.

Important peoples → Dorze, Wolaita, Yem, Kafa, Dizi, Bench, Ari, Dasanach, Tsamayi, Erbore, Hamar, Surma, Nyangatom, Bodi, Male and others.

📌 Important feature → development of highly organized indigenous political systems.

title: 8.1.1.1 👑 Omotic States under the Tato System
notes:
Kafa, Shekka and Yem → developed elaborate state structures ruled by kings using the title Tato.

👑 Yem → located between the Gibe and upper Omo Rivers; center at Angar Fochara. Kings were political and religious leaders. Economy → mainly enset, barley and sorghum; trade and handicrafts were secondary.

👑 Kafa → south of Gojeb River; Minjo dynasty ruled from about 1390. Capital → Bonga. Tato had strong authority and was assisted by the Council of Seven, Mikkerecho. Economy → agriculture + trade; exports included ivory, cattle, musk, slaves and later coffee.

🛡️ Kafa → used watchtowers, trenches and natural defenses; resisted Oromo expansion for a long period.

👑 Shekka → west of Kafa and east of Baro River. Batto dynasty was followed by Bushasho dynasty. Capital → Gecha. Ruled by Tato and frequently fought the Macha Oromo.

title: 8.1.1.2 🛡️ Omotic States under the Kawo/Kati System
notes:
Wolaita → south of the former Sultanate of Hadya; connected historically with Damot.

👑 Wolaita rulers → used title Kawo. The Kawo possessed extensive authority over people and land.

⚔️ Warrior class → Goqa.
🌾 Economy → agriculture, with trade and handicrafts as supplementary activities.
🧱 Ijajo Kalla → dry-stone defensive walls of Wolaita.

👑 Dawuro → located around the Omo basin. The Kawuka dynasty united many petty chiefdoms around 1700. Kings used title Kati.

🧱 Kati Halala Kalla → defensive walls associated with Kati Halala.

🌾 Gamo → economy based on agriculture; communities were organized into independent Darie units, each ruled by a hereditary Kawo.

👑 Gofa → independent kingdom with sacred kings. Administration included a highland Kawo/Kati and lowland rain king, Ira-Kati. Customary law → Woga.

📌 Other peoples with similar Kawo/Kati structures → Zayse, Basketo, Oyda, Kara, Malle and Kore.

title: 8.1.1.3 ⚖️ Cushitic Peoples under the Sera-Woma System
notes:
Major peoples → Sidama, Hadya, Kambata, Tambaro, Halaba, Qabena and others.

🌾 Economy → mainly agriculture, especially enset and coffee.

Sera-Woma → indigenous governance and conflict-resolution system dealing with disputes over property, marriage and homicide.

👥 Sidama:
Woma → village-level cultural and ritual leadership.
Sera → customary social constitution/law.
Luwa → generation-set system; grades rotated periodically.

Luwa grades → Wawassa → Darara → Mogissa → Hirbora → Fullassa.

📅 Fiche Chamballalla → Sidama New Year associated with the rotation of Luwa grades.

👥 Kambata:
Sera → indigenous governing institution.
Hambarcho → seven-member council representing the seven clans; performed administrative and judicial functions.

title: 8.1.1.4 👥 Gedeo, Konso and Gurage
notes:
🌿 Gedeo → lived east of Lake Abaya; closely related historically to Guji Oromo and linguistically close to Sidama. Main economy → enset cultivation.

Ballee → Gedeo council of elders working through age classes and ranking.
7 grades × 10 years → 70-year cycle.

🏔️ Konso → Cushitic-speaking people of southwest Ethiopia.
Economy → agriculture.
Major achievements → terracing + soil conservation + wooden carvings + stone enclosures.
Hayyota → village council of elders; membership rotated rather than being hereditary.
Tsella → generation-set organization.

👥 Gurage → major groups included Sabat Bet and Kestane.
Economy → mainly enset.
No centralized political authority → lineage-based customary governance.

⚖️ Yajoka Qicha → important Sabat Bet political/judicial institution.
⚖️ Gordanna Sera → important Kestane political/judicial institution.

📌 Both assemblies combined rule-making and judicial functions and could act as supreme courts.

title: 8.1.2 🌾 Western States — Gibe and Leqa Oromo
notes:
The Gibe Valley and Wallaga were increasingly occupied by Macha Oromo groups during the late 16th and 17th centuries.

Earlier states such as Bizamo, Ennarya and Anfillo declined or disappeared; Shekka came under strong Macha Oromo pressure.

🔄 By about 1800 → Gibe Oromo changed from Gadaa governance toward monarchy.

Main causes → revival of long-distance trade + spread of Islam + rise of powerful Abbaa Duulaa + wealth from agriculture, tribute, taxation, trade and war booty.

💰 Wealth allowed war leaders to maintain permanent armies and become Mootii (kings).

Five Gibe Monarchies → Limmu-Ennarya + Jimma-Kakka + Gera + Gomma + Gumma.

Major trade goods → ivory + musk + spices + skins + slaves + gold + coffee.

📌 Trade routes were a major foundation of Gibe prosperity.

title: 8.1.2.1 👑 The Gibe Monarchies
notes:
👑 Limmu-Ennarya → formed around 1800 by the Limmu Macha Oromo on the former Ennarya kingdom. First king → Bofo/Abba Gomol I. Capital → Saqqa. Reached greatest power under Ibsa/Abba Bagibo.

👑 Gumma → state formation completed around 1810 by Oncho Jilcha.

👑 Gomma → state formation strengthened by Abba Manno. Islamized by the 1830s; Islam helped strengthen the dynasty.

👑 Jimma-Kakka → established around 1830 by Sanna, later Abba Jiffar I. Controlled important trade routes. Abba Jiffar I became the first Muslim king of Jimma. Capital → Hirmata.

👑 Gera → founded around the mid-1830s by Tullu Gunji. Later ruled by Abba Baso and Abba Rago.

title: 8.1.2.2 🏹 Leeqa Oromo States
notes:
Leeqa groups → located in present-day Wallaga, east of the Didessa River.

Main states → Leeqa Naqamtee + Leeqa Qellam.

🔄 Political transformation → similar to the Gibe region; powerful Abbaa Duulaa challenged Gadaa authority.

👤 Bakaree Godana → unified families around Naqamtee and established a strong polity based on agriculture.
👤 Moroda Bakaree → expanded influence through war and diplomacy.

👤 Tulluu → unified Leeqa Qellam groups and built a strong polity based on agriculture and gold trade with Sudan.

Trade connections → Assossa + Benishangul + Sudan.

title: 8.1.2.3 🕌 Benishangul-Gumuz Sheikhdoms
notes:
Indigenous peoples → Benishangul (Berta) and Gumuz.

19th century Muslim Sheikhdoms → Assossa (Aqoldi) + Benishangul + Khomosha.

Main factors for their rise → Islam from Sudan + trans-border trade + abundant gold and natural resources.

🏜️ Gubba → another Sheikhdom that emerged in Gumuz-inhabited Metekkel during the 19th century.

📌 Gold and strategic location attracted Egyptian and Sudanese expansion.

title: 8.1.2.4 🌿 Gambella Peoples and Local Chiefs
notes:
Five major peoples before the mid-19th century → Nuer + Anywaa + Majang + Opuo + Komo.

Languages → Eastern Sudanic branch of the Nilo-Saharan super-family.

🌾 Anywaa, Opuo, Komo → mainly settled agriculture + fishing + hunting + gathering.
🐄 Nuer → pastoralism was the economic foundation; social status was strongly connected with cattle ownership.
🌿 Majang → shifting cultivation + hunting and gathering.

👥 Anywaa political system → each village had a Kwaari (village headman) and Nyiye (noble).

Nuer political organization → lacked formal centralized authority; spiritual leaders included Khor Muon (peacemaking), Khor Touch (water) and Khor Tang (war).

title: 8.1.3 🕌 Eastern States — Harar
notes:
Harar → major political, commercial and Islamic center in eastern Ethiopia.

1552–1553 → Emir Nur ibn al-Wazir built the Jugol wall around Harar.

1577 → pressure from Barantu Oromo forced the Adal political center to move from Harar to Aussa.

👑 Emir Ali Dawud (r.1647–1662) → founder and first ruler of the local Harari dynasty that declared independence.

Harar then became a major trade center for about two centuries.

Trade routes → Zeyla and Berbera ↔ interior Ethiopian region.

💰 Harar → minted its own coins from the 17th century.

🕌 Harar → important center of Islamic learning and culture.

title: 8.1.3.1 🤝 Harari, Oromo, Somali and Afar Interactions
notes:
Harar's trade created strong economic interdependence among Harari, Oromo, Somali, Afar and other peoples.

🌾 Oromo → supplied grain, fruits and vegetables.
🔨 Harari → produced handicrafts.
🐪 Somali and Afar → brought animals for exchange.

Main forces of integration → economic links + marriage relations + Islam.

🏛️ Important Harari institutions:
Afocha → self-help association and conflict-resolution institution.
Aboch → male Afocha.
Endoch → female Afocha.

📌 Afocha promoted cooperation, mediation, social solidarity and an egalitarian spirit.

title: 8.1.3.2 🐪 Afar Sultanates
notes:
Afar → ancient Cushitic-speaking people; mainly pastoralists.

Four major Afar Sultanates → Tajura + Rahayito + Aussa + Goba'ad.

👑 Aussa Imamate → leading political center of the Afar; other Afar sultanates nominally recognized its primacy.

🚢 Tajura → important strategic and economic center.

19th-century trade exports through Tajura → slaves + ivory + gold + wheat + durra + honey + civet + ostrich feathers.

⚖️ Makabonto → indigenous Afar court system.
Makaban → judge knowledgeable in Afar customary law.
Number of judges → varied according to seriousness of the case.

title: 8.1.3.3 🐪 Somali People
notes:
Somali people → mainly inhabited the Ogaden region.

Language → Eastern Lowland Cushitic.

Economy → mainly pastoralism; also agriculture and trade.

📜 Earlier inhabitants of Ogaden → Harla, whose ruins of stone-built houses remain in parts of the region.

14th–16th centuries → Ogaden was influenced by Ifat and later Adal.

By the beginning of the 16th century → Somali communities had largely adopted Islam through Muslim merchants.

👥 Indigenous political institution → Shir, a council of elders.

Shir responsibilities → criminal and civil cases + resource allocation + marriage + trade + community affairs.

title: 8.2 👑 Instability versus Consolidation in the Christian Highland Kingdom, 1559–1855
notes:
After the wars of Imam Ahmad → the Christian Highland Kingdom struggled to recover.

Major stages:
1559–early 17th century → attempts at consolidation + political instability.

1636–1769 → Gondarine Period → cultural revival and royal splendor.

1769–1855 → Zemene Mesafint → Era of Warlords and weakening central authority.

📌 Major issues → Oromo expansion + Ottoman pressure + royal succession conflicts + Catholic controversy + regional lord rivalry.

title: 8.2.1 🧭 Attempts at Consolidation and New Political Geography
notes:
👑 King Minas (r.1559–1563) → shifted the political center toward the Lake Tana region.

Political centers moved → Shewan highlands → Mengiste Semayat in East Gojjam → Dembiya near Lake Tana.

Main reasons:
• Oromo expansion south of the Abay.
• Ottoman occupation of Massawa in 1557.
• Ottoman advance into the interior.
• Regional rebellions and rivalry among warlords.

📍 Lake Tana region advantages → fertile agriculture + tribute collection + military settlement + revived trade.

👑 Sertse Dingil → capital at Emfraz; palace at Guzara.
👑 Susenyos → capitals at Gorgora and Denqez; secondary center at Yibaba.

📌 These developments helped prepare the way for Gondar as a permanent capital.

title: 8.2.2 ✝️ Imposition of Catholicism and the Jesuit Mission
notes:
Portugal and the Pope of Rome wanted to convert Ethiopia to Catholicism after the decline of Adal's power.

Jesuits → members of the Society of Jesus, established as part of the Catholic Counter-Reformation.

👑 Gelawdewos → rejected Catholic conversion and defended Orthodox practices.

👤 Andre de Oviedo → arrived in 1557 but failed to convert Gelawdewos.

👤 Pedro Paez → arrived in 1603; successfully influenced many important figures and eventually converted King Susenyos.

👑 Susenyos → increasingly supported Catholicism partly to obtain Portuguese military assistance.

1622 → Susenyos officially became Catholic and made Catholicism the state religion.

⚔️ Consequences → Orthodox clergy and peasants resisted; religious controversy produced rebellions, violence and civil conflict.

👤 Alfonso Mendez → arrived in 1625 and continued the Catholic mission.

1632 → Susenyos abandoned Catholicism; his son Fasiledes restored the Orthodox Church and expelled the Jesuits.

title: 8.2.2.1 🛑 Why Catholicism Failed
notes:
Major reasons:
• Strong resistance from Orthodox clergy.
• Opposition from peasants and nobility.
• Rapid imposition of Catholic practices.
• Banning of long-established Ethiopian Christian practices such as Saturday observance, fasting and circumcision.
• Portuguese military assistance expected by Susenyos failed to arrive.
• Catholicism became associated with foreign interference.

📌 Final result → Susenyos abandoned Catholicism in 1632; Fasiledes restored Orthodoxy and expelled Jesuit missionaries.

title: 8.2.2.2 🚪 Fasiledes and the Closed-Door Policy
notes:
👑 Fasiledes → restored the Orthodox Church after becoming king in 1632.

He concluded agreements with Muslim rulers of Yemen, Swakin and Massawa to prevent or report European entry into the Christian kingdom.

🚪 Closed-door policy → restricted European contact with Ethiopia.

Purpose → protect the kingdom from external interference and avoid another religious conflict.

The policy continued until the beginning of the 19th century.

Only a few Europeans reached the royal court during the isolation period, including Charles Jacques Poncet and James Bruce.

title: 8.2.3 🏰 The Gondarine Period, 1636–1769
notes:
👑 Fasiledes → established Gondar as a permanent capital around 1636.

Gondar became the political + economic + intellectual + religious + cultural center of the kingdom.

🏛️ Achievements:
• Castles and palaces.
• Churches and royal residences.
• Architecture combining Aksumite, Zagwe and later influences.
• Church education.
• Poetry and theology.
• Painting and calligraphy.
• Cross-making and other crafts.

🛒 Economy → active markets and trade routes connected Gondar with southwestern Ethiopia, Massawa and Metemma.

📌 Gondar's cultural revival became one of the most important features of the period.

title: 8.2.3.1 👑 Major Gondarine Rulers
notes:
👑 Fasiledes (1632–1667) → established Gondar as permanent capital around 1636; restored Orthodoxy.

👑 Yohannis I (1667–1682) → one of the major early Gondarine rulers.

👑 Iyasu I / Iyasu the Great (1682–1706) → last especially powerful Gondarine ruler.

Major achievements of Iyasu I → military campaigns + revision of Fitha Negest + land-law reforms + reorganization of taxes and customs + promotion of trade.

📌 Iyasu's reign also saw renewed contact with Europeans, including physician Jacques Poncet.

title: 8.2.3.2 👑 Mintiwab and the Rise of Regional Rivalry
notes:
After Iyasu I → political disorder increased; kings were frequently murdered or overthrown.

👑 Bekaffa (1721–1730) → period of relative stability.

👑 Iyasu II (1730–1755) → ruled under the regency of his mother, Etege Mintiwab.

👑 Etege Mintiwab → powerful female political figure who exercised major influence over government.

Her power was strengthened through:
• Political alliances.
• Marriage connections.
• Appointment of relatives and supporters.
• Support from Quara elites.
• Construction of churches and gaining support of clergy and people.

👑 Iyo'as (1755–1769) → Oromo influence in Gondar increased because of his maternal connection with Wollo Oromo.

📌 Rivalry between Quaregnoch and Yejju Oromo factions contributed directly to the crisis that preceded the Zemene Mesafint.

title: 8.2.4 ⚔️ Zemene Mesafint — Era of Warlords, 1769–1855
notes:
Zemene Mesafint → period of weakened central authority and strong regional warlords.

📅 Beginning → 1769, following the murder of Iyo'as.
📅 End → 1855.

Main features:
• Weak central monarchy.
• Powerful regional lords.
• Frequent civil wars.
• Political rivalry.
• Lawlessness and insecurity.
• Regionalism.
• Religious disputes.
• Kings became largely powerless.

👑 Rasbitweded → powerful king-makers who could appoint or remove kings.

📌 Actual power → increasingly held by regional Rases and Dejjazmaches with their own armies and revenues.

title: 8.2.4.1 🧩 Causes of the Zemene Mesafint
notes:
Major causes:

⚔️ 1. Long-term effects of Imam Ahmad's wars → weakened the military and political authority of the monarchy.

🏹 2. Oromo expansion → several kings suffered military defeats and lost control of territories.

🏰 3. Permanent capital at Gondar → kings became more distant from provinces while regional lords increased their power.

👑 4. Rivalry among regional nobles → powerful lords competed to control the throne and obtain the position of Rasbitweded.

⛪ 5. Religious disputes → divisions within the Orthodox Church weakened its unifying role.

🏛️ 6. Weak administration → regional governors increasingly made their positions hereditary.

📌 Result → central authority declined while regional political power increased.

title: 8.2.4.2 🐎 Yejju Oromo Influence
notes:
After the decline of Ras Michael Sehul → Yejju Oromo nobles became dominant in the central regions.

1786 → Yejju/Werre Sheh dynasty established.

👤 Ali Gwangul (Ali I) → founder of the Yejju political dynasty and Rasbitweded.

Important Yejju leaders → Ras Gugsa + Ras Ali Alula (Ras Ali II).

📍 Center of influence → Debre Tabor and Gondar.

📌 Yejju Oromo hegemony became one of the defining political features of the Zemene Mesafint.

title: 8.2.4.3 📉 Effects of the Zemene Mesafint
notes:
👨‍🌾 Peasants → forced to fight in wars; farms were destroyed or became battlefields; crops were looted.

🏴 Shifta → some people abandoned normal occupations and became bandits.

🛒 Merchants → faced robbery and multiple taxes at regional customs posts.

🔨 Handicrafts → disrupted by continuous warfare.

📉 Overall effects → decline in agricultural production + stagnation of trade + collapse of handicrafts + poverty + insecurity + political fragmentation.

🌍 Foreign pressure → Egyptian expansion from Sudan increased after Muhammad Ali extended Egyptian rule over Sudan in 1821.

title: 8.2.4.4 🏆 End of the Zemene Mesafint — Tewodros II
notes:
👤 Kasa Hailu → later Emperor Tewodros II.

He defeated major regional rulers in a series of decisive battles:

⚔️ 1852 → Battle of Gur Amba → defeated Dejjazmach Goshu Zewde.

⚔️ 1853 → Battle of Gorgora Bichen → defeated forces of Ras Ali II.

⚔️ June 1853 → Battle of Ayshal → defeated Ras Ali II.

⚔️ 1855 → Battle of Deresge → defeated Dejjazmach Wube of Tigray and Semien.

👑 1855 → Kasa Hailu crowned Emperor Tewodros II.

📌 Significance → began the process of restoring strong central authority and ended the Zemene Mesafint.

title: 8.2.5 🏹 Kingdom of Shewa
notes:
👑 Negasi Kirstos → founded the Shewan dynasty at the end of the 17th century; claimed descent from King Libne Dingil.

Political centers:
Ayne → early center.
Doqaqit → established under Abiye.
Ankober → established as center by Meridazmach Amhayesus.

During the Zemene Mesafint → Shewa remained relatively independent and avoided the major northern civil wars.

👑 Asfawossen (1775–1808) → expanded Shewa and strengthened administration.

👤 Abegazoch → governors appointed over major regions.

👑 Wossenseged (1808–1813) → strengthened administration, promoted marriage ties with Oromo and followed religious tolerance and social equality.

👑 Sahle Selassie (1813–1847) → Shewa reached its highest degree of autonomy; expanded south and southwest and developed trade and foreign relations.

title: 8.2.5.1 🌍 Sahle Selassie and Foreign Relations
notes:
👑 Sahle Selassie → wanted to strengthen and modernize Shewa.

Main interests → firearms + medicine + crafts + arts + construction + mechanical technology.

Foreign visitors during his reign included:
• Combes and Tamisier.
• Krapf and Isenberg.
• Rochet d'Hericourt.
• Major W.C. Harris.

📜 Treaties:
1841 → trade and friendship treaty with Major W.C. Harris.
1843 → similar treaty with Rochet d'Hericourt.

📈 Result → expansion of Shewa + increased trade + greater political autonomy + stronger foreign contacts.

title: 8.2.6 🌍 European Travelers, Explorers and Missionaries since 1805
notes:
19th-century foreigners came to Ethiopia for different reasons:

🔬 Scientific research.
✝️ Religious missionary activity.
🗺️ Adventure and exploration.
🤝 Diplomatic relations.
🛒 Trade and commercial interests.
🔫 Access to firearms and political influence.

📌 A major historical significance → foreign contacts helped prepare the way for wider European political and colonial interests in Africa.

👤 Henry Salt → reached the court of Ras Wolde Sellassie in 1805.

Other visitors → Samuel Gobat + Christian Kugler + C.W. Isenberg + De Jacobis + Cardinal Massaja + Eduard Ruppell + Abbadie brothers + W.C. Harris + John Bell + Walter Plowden.

title: 8.2.6.1 📜 Treaties with Foreigners
notes:
👑 Ethiopian regional rulers sought foreign relations mainly to obtain firearms and strengthen political power.

Important agreements:

📜 1841 → W.C. Harris + Nigus Sahle Selassie → treaty of commerce and friendship.

📜 1843 → Rochet d'Hericourt + Nigus Sahle Selassie → treaty of commerce/friendship.

📜 1849 → Walter Plowden + Ras Ali II → treaty of friendship.

📌 Ethiopian rulers → wanted firearms, technology, medicine, skilled workers and political/diplomatic support.

📌 Europeans → sought information, influence, trade, religious opportunities and wider strategic interests.

title: 🏆 UNIT 8 — MUST REMEMBER
notes:
🌿 SOUTHERN STATES

Omotic → organized indigenous states.

Tato → title used by Kafa, Shekka and Yem rulers.

Kawo/Kati → important Omotic royal system.

Kafa → Bonga + Tato + Mikkerecho + trade + strong defenses.

Wolaita → Kawo + Goqa + Ijajo Kalla.

Dawuro → Kawuka dynasty + Kati Halala Kalla.

Gamo → Darie + hereditary Kawo.

Gofa → Kawo/Kati + Ira-Kati + Woga.

⚖️ SERA-WOMA

Sidama → Woma + Sera + Luwa.

Luwa grades → Wawassa → Darara → Mogissa → Hirbora → Fullassa.

Kambata → Sera + Hambarcho.

Gedeo → Ballee + seven grades + 70-year cycle.

Konso → Hayyota + Tsella + terracing.

Gurage → Yajoka Qicha + Gordanna Sera.

🏹 WESTERN STATES

Gibe Monarchies → Limmu-Ennarya + Jimma-Kakka + Gera + Gomma + Gumma.

Main causes of monarchy → trade + Islam + Abbaa Duulaa + wealth + permanent armies.

Main trade goods → coffee + gold + ivory + musk + spices + skins.

Benishangul-Gumuz → Assossa + Benishangul + Khomosha + Gubba.

Main causes → Islam + Sudan trade + gold.

Gambella → Nuer + Anywaa + Majang + Opuo + Komo.

🕌 EASTERN STATES

Harar → Jugol wall + trade + Islam + Afocha.

1577 → Adal political center moved to Aussa.

Ali Dawud → independent Harari dynasty.

Afar → Aussa + Tajura + Rahayito + Goba'ad.

Somali → Ogaden + Islam + Shir council.

👑 CHRISTIAN HIGHLAND KINGDOM

1559 → Minas shifted center toward Lake Tana.

Lake Tana → fertile + strategic + trade + tribute.

✝️ CATHOLICISM

Gelawdewos → rejected conversion.

Pedro Paez → influential Catholic missionary.

Susenyos → converted to Catholicism in 1622.

Alfonso Mendez → arrived in 1625.

1632 → Susenyos abandoned Catholicism.

Fasiledes → restored Orthodoxy + expelled Jesuits + closed-door policy.

🏰 GONDAR
1636 → Gondar permanent capital under Fasiledes.

Major features → castles + churches + painting + education + trade + cultural revival.

Iyasu I → reforms + military campaigns + trade.

Mintiwab → major female political figure.

⚔️ ZEMENE MESAFINT
1769–1855 → Era of Warlords.

Main features → weak monarchy + powerful regional lords + civil wars + regionalism.

Rasbitweded → king-maker.

Yejju Oromo → major political influence.

Effects → agricultural decline + trade disruption + poverty + insecurity.

🏆 END
1852 → Gur Amba.

1853 → Gorgora Bichen + Ayshal.

1855 → Deresge.

1855 → Kasa Hailu became Emperor Tewodros II.

🏹 SHEWA

Negasi Kirstos → founder.

Abiye → expansion.

Amhayesus → Ankober.

Asfawossen → administration and expansion.

Wossenseged → religious tolerance + social equality.

Sahle Selassie → highest autonomy + foreign relations.

🌍 EUROPEANS

1805 → Henry Salt.

1841 → Harris–Sahle Selassie treaty.

1843 → Rochet d'Hericourt–Sahle Selassie treaty.

1849 → Plowden–Ras Ali II treaty.

🧠 EXAM CONNECTION:

Tato → Kafa, Shekka, Yem.

Kawo/Kati → Wolaita, Dawuro, Gamo, Gofa and related Omotic states.

Sera-Woma → Sidama, Kambata and related southern Cushitic societies.

Gibe monarchy → trade + Islam + war leaders.

Harar → trade + Islam + Afocha.

Gondar → permanent capital + cultural revival.

Zemene Mesafint → weak central authority + regional warlords.

Tewodros II → ended Zemene Mesafint and began centralization.
